gbs333-aa6516-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether God under the proper aspect of deity is the subject of theology.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e125.summary: Outlines the question's structure in two articles: the first, after reciting and rejecting Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prol. q. 3), shows what belongs to the notion of the first subject of a science and how one science has one subject; the second, after some suppositions, answers the question.
claims: Article 1 treats the notion of the subject of a science against Scotus; article 2 answers the question about theology's subject.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e148.summary: Presents Scotus's view: the notion of a first subject is to contain virtually and first all the truths of the habit. 'Containing virtually' means containing causally, i.e., being able to cause, as knowledge of premises virtually contains knowledge of the conclusion. Scotus argues that the first subject contains the immediate propositions (since the subject contains the predicate and so the evidence of the whole proposition), and immediate propositions contain the conclusions, so the subject contains all the habit's truths.
claims: (Scotus) The first subject of a science virtually contains all the truths of that science.
(Scotus) Virtual containment is causal containment: the power to cause another cognition.
(Scotus) The subject contains its immediate propositions, which contain the conclusions.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e192.summary: First argument against Scotus: no incomplex cognition of one thing, together with the intellect, is ever a sufficient cause of the first incomplex cognition of another thing. Experience shows that however perfectly one intuitively knows one thing, one never thereby has proper incomplex knowledge of another; such knowledge is intuitive, which can naturally only be caused by the thing itself, or abstractive, which presupposes intuitive cognition. So a blind man cannot have distinct proper knowledge of colors.
claims: No incomplex cognition of one thing suffices to cause the first incomplex cognition of another.
Intuitive cognition can naturally be caused only by its object.
Abstractive cognition presupposes intuitive cognition.
A blind person cannot have proper distinct cognition of colors.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e227.summary: Second point against Scotus: a subject does not always virtually contain its attribute, because attributes frequently connote things really distinct from their subjects and not virtually contained in them.
claims: A subject does not always virtually contain its attribute.
Attributes often connote things really distinct from the subject.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e240.summary: Third point: distinct knowledge of subject and attribute does not always virtually contain knowledge of the immediate proposition composed of them, since experience is often required. 'Heat is heat-producing' is immediate, yet however distinctly one knows heat and heating, without experience one no more knows that heat heats than that whiteness produces whiteness; similarly for man and risible.
claims: Distinct knowledge of the terms does not always yield knowledge of the immediate proposition.
Some immediate propositions, like 'heat is heat-producing', are known only by experience.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e271.summary: Fourth point: it is not part of the notion of a subject of science that it virtually contains its attributes.
claims: Virtually containing its attributes is not part of the notion of a subject of science.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e280.summary: Fifth point: it is not part of the notion of a subject that the science is named and specified by it, because there can be distinct sciences of the same subject in thing and reason owing to diverse attributes. Nor does a science derive its dignity from its subject, since with the same subject one science may be nobler because of the nobility of its attributes, as knowledge that man is beatifiable is nobler than knowledge that man is risible or mortal.
claims: Sciences are not specified by their subjects; distinct sciences can share a subject.
A science's dignity can derive from its attributes rather than its subject.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e310.summary: Sixth point: it is not part of the notion of the subject that it be what first occurs to the intellect in that science, with other things under its aspect. An attribute can be prior to the subject in generation and in perfection, since accidents and operations signified by attributes are often better known than the substance signified by the subject, and the form signified by an attribute of matter is more perfect than matter.
claims: The subject need not be the first thing known in a science.
Attributes can be prior to the subject in order of knowledge and perfection.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e339.summary: Seventh point: it is not part of the notion of the subject that it be the first mover, or first reason moving the intellect, to all the knowledge to which the habit inclines.
claims: The subject need not be the first mover of the intellect to all the science's knowledge.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e348.summary: Eighth point: nor is it required that knowledge of the subject be principally intended, since knowledge of the whole proposition is principally intended; and sometimes the subject is equally well known beforehand. The moon, for instance, is not known more perfectly by knowing that it is eclipsed, but something else about it is known that was not known before.
claims: Knowledge of the whole proposition, not of the subject, is principally intended in science.
Scientific knowledge adds knowledge about the subject, not more perfect knowledge of it.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e368.summary: Ockham's positive account: nothing more is required for the subject of a science than that it be the subject of the known proposition, so that the subject of a science is the subject of the known conclusion. Proof: science cannot be had without knowledge of its subject, but can be had without knowledge of anything other than the premises, conclusion, and their terms (subject, middle, predicate); since the subject is neither a premise, conclusion, middle, nor predicate, it is the subject of the conclusion. Hence an aggregately one science has as many subjects as conclusions with diverse subjects, though these may be ordered by predication (commonness), perfection, or totality, and one first among them is often assigned as the subject. As aggregate science is not truly one science, it has not one subject simply but many, one of which may be first in some way.
claims: The subject of a science is just the subject of the known conclusion.
An aggregate science has as many subjects as its conclusions have diverse subjects.
Among these subjects there may be orders of predication, perfection, and totality.
An aggregate science has no single subject simply, though one may be first in some order.
concepts: subject of science as subject of conclusion

gbs333-aa6516-d1e438.summary: Restates the account more clearly, with a first supposition: by 'subject' is meant a simple term, incomplex at least with respect to propositional complexity, since the subject is that of which attributes are predicated and thus an extreme of a proposition or conclusion.
claims: The subject of a science is a term incomplex with respect to propositional composition.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e460.summary: Second supposition and argument: the subject is not, properly speaking, in the science as part of it, since science is an adhesive habitual or actual knowledge of a demonstrable conclusion, a simple quality not composed of parts of diverse kinds (only of intensive degrees), whereas the subject's knowledge is apprehensive and of a different kind. A subject is 'of' a science as something required for the science's being or becoming. Since nothing more is required, besides the intellect and God's general influence, than premises, conclusion, assent to premises, and their terms, and the subject is none of the propositions or assents, it is a term; of the three terms of a demonstration it is neither middle nor predicate (usually the attribute), so it is the conclusion's subject. Thus there are as many subjects as known conclusions with diverse subjects; among them an order of predication and perfection lets one be called first, the 'subject of attribution' of the total science, usually the more common and less connotative term, which saves what the moderns say about the subject of attribution.
claims: Science is a simple quality of adhesion to a conclusion, composed only of intensive degrees.
The subject is not a part of the science but a requisite for it.
Generation of science requires only intellect, God's general concurrence, premises, conclusion, assent to premises, and terms.
The subject of a science is the subject of its conclusion.
The 'subject of attribution' of an aggregate science is the first in an order of predication or perfection, typically the most common and least connotative.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e572.summary: Second article. Supposes that 'subject' is taken either as subject of predication or of inherence, only the former being relevant. Subject of predication means either the extreme of a proposition (the term or concept of which the predicate is said) or the signified thing for which that term supposits.
claims: 'Subject' here means subject of predication, not of inherence.
Subject of predication is either the term itself or the thing for which it supposits.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e594.summary: Further suppositions: the subject of a science differs from its object, the object being the known conclusion of which the subject is a part. Referring to d. 3 q. 2 and Prologue qq. 1–2, God cannot naturally be known by us in via in himself or distinctly (with nothing else terminating the act), but only in a concept common to him and creatures, or in a composite concept proper to him whose parts belong also to creatures, such as 'highest infinite being'. And, from qq. 1 and 8, science is taken either as a simple habit or aggregatively, and theology as that of wayfarers or of the blessed.
claims: The object of a science is the known conclusion; the subject is part of the object.
God cannot be naturally known in himself in this life, only through common or composite proper concepts.
Science may be a simple habit or an aggregate; theology may be of wayfarers or of the blessed.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e655.summary: First and second conclusions. First: taking the subject as the thing signified for which the subject term supposits, in some part of theology God under the aspect of deity is the subject, in another the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or a creature, since the subject is what the conclusion's subject supposits for, and this varies across conclusions. Second: taking the subject as the suppositing term, neither God nor any extra-mental thing that is not a sign is the subject of theology, whether total or partial.
claims: Taking subject as significate, God under the aspect of deity is the subject of some parts of theology, while the persons or creatures are subjects of others.
Taking subject as term, neither God nor any extramental non-sign thing is the subject of theology.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e688.summary: Third conclusion: different parts of theology have different subjects, and sometimes one subject when diverse attributes are demonstrated of one subject in diverse conclusions.
claims: Different parts of theology have different subjects.
One subject may serve where several attributes are shown of it.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e701.summary: Notes that similar conclusions can be posed for the theology of the blessed, whose subjects likewise vary with the diversity of its cognitions and conclusions.
claims: The theology of the blessed also has diverse subjects according to its diverse conclusions.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e712.summary: Asks what the first subject of theology taken aggregatively is: according to different kinds of primacy, different first subjects can be assigned. God under the aspect of deity is first in perfection relative to creatures, and in some priority relative to the persons; Christ can be first by priority of containment, since he contains divine and created nature; 'things and signs' can be first by priority of commonness, since everything treated in theology is a thing or a sign. But God as redeemer or as glorifier is not the subject, since these aspects belong to predicates ('God is redeemer'), not to the subject.
claims: Theology taken aggregatively has different first subjects according to different kinds of primacy.
God under the aspect of deity is first in perfection.
Christ is first by containment, as uniting divine and created nature.
Res et signa are first by commonness.
God as redeemer or glorifier is not the subject, since these are predicate-side aspects.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e768.summary: Asks what theology is about. Theology is taken in one sense as knowledge of theological truth by infused faith, in another as the simply theological habit including acquired faith (q. 8, q. 1). In the first sense theology is not about all things, complex or incomplex, since it concerns only infused faith, which is one in the Fathers and in us, as taught in Book III.
claims: Theology as infused faith is not about all things, complex or incomplex.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e794.summary: In the second sense, theology is about all things signified by the terms of theological propositions; and since there is no term of which some theological attribute cannot be predicated (every being is creator or creature, creatable, annihilable, etc.), theology is about all incomplexes. But it is not about all complexes, i.e., all conclusions as proximate knowables, since not all demonstrable conclusions, such as metaphysical or logical ones, are demonstrated in theology.
claims: Acquired theology is about everything signified by terms of theological propositions.
Every term admits some theological predicate (e.g. creature, creatable, annihilable).
Theology covers all incomplexes but not all conclusions; metaphysical and logical conclusions are not demonstrated in it.

gbs333-aa6516-d1e827.summary: Corollary: in this second sense theology treats every being in particular: God as creator of all and most common cause, and creatures as God's works and effects. Refers to Scotus, prologue q. 3, and introduces the third part of the prologue with q. 10.
claims: Theology treats every being, God as universal cause and creatures as his effects.

gbs333-aa6516.summary: Quaestio 9 opens the second part of the prologue on the subject of theology, asking whether God under the proper aspect of deity is theology's subject. Article 1 attacks Scotus's view that a science's first subject virtually contains all its truths. In Ockham's empiricist terms, no incomplex cognition of one thing suffices to cause cognition of another, since abstractive knowledge presupposes intuitive knowledge. Subjects do not always virtually contain their attributes, and knowledge of the terms does not yield knowledge of some immediate propositions without experience. Nor is the subject what specifies a science or gives it dignity, what is first known, what first moves the intellect, or what is principally intended. Positively, the subject of a science is just the subject of its known conclusion: science is a simple quality of assent, the subject is a requisite term rather than a part, and an aggregate science has as many subjects as its conclusions, one of which may be called the 'subject of attribution' by some order of primacy. Article 2 distinguishes subject as term from subject as significate and recalls that God is known in via only by common or composite concepts. It concludes that, as significate, God under deity is the subject of some parts of theology and the persons or creatures of others, while as term no extramental thing is theology's subject. Different parts have different subjects, and for theology as a whole God under deity (by perfection), Christ (by containment), or things and signs (by commonness) may each be called first, but not God as redeemer or glorifier. Acquired theology concerns all incomplexes, since every being is creator or creature, but not all conclusions.
claims: Against Scotus, the subject of a science does not virtually contain all the science's truths.
The subject of a science is simply the subject of the known conclusion; aggregate sciences have many subjects.

As significate, God under the aspect of deity is the subject of some parts of theology, while other parts have the divine persons or creatures as subject; as term, no extramental thing is theology's subject.
Different first subjects of theology may be assigned by different kinds of primacy: God (perfection), Christ (containment), res et signa (commonness).
Acquired theology concerns every incomplex but not every demonstrable conclusion.
concepts: subject as subject of the conclusion
